questions.q: A 35-year-old farmer presents with a painless nodule on the right hand that ulcerated and developed a black eschar with surrounding marked non-pitting oedema. No fever or systemic symptoms. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: The painless black eschar with gelatinous non-pitting oedema (malignant pustule) in a farmer with animal contact is classic for cutaneous anthrax caused by Bacillus anthracis. The oedema is due to anthrax toxins.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with whitish plaques on the buccal mucosa that can be scraped off, leaving a raw bleeding surface. KOH mount shows pseudohyphae and budding yeasts. Which virulence factor of the causative organism helps it adhere to epithelial cells?
questions.exp: Candida albicans uses Als (agglutinin-like sequence) glycoproteins as adhesins to bind to host epithelial and endothelial cells. This is the primary adhesion mechanism. Phospholipase B aids tissue invasion, mannoprotein modulates immunity, and ergosterol is a membrane sterol.

questions.q: A 22-year-old presents with grouped vesicles on the glans penis recurring for the third time in 6 months. He reports burning prodrome before each episode. The drug that reduces the frequency of recurrences by the greatest amount when used as suppressive therapy is:
questions.exp: Valacyclovir 1 g OD as daily suppressive therapy for recurrent genital herpes reduces recurrence frequency by approximately 78% and also significantly reduces viral shedding and transmission to uninfected partners. It is the highest-efficacy suppressive regimen.

questions.q: A 30-year-old Indian patient has multiple hypopigmented patches with loss of sensation, and a thickened great auricular nerve. Slit-skin smear from an active lesion shows solid-staining bacilli. The Ridley-Jopling classification and lepromin reaction of this patient would most likely be:
questions.exp: Solid-staining bacilli on SSS indicate high bacillary load (high BI), placing this patient at the lepromatous end. BL leprosy has high BI, negative lepromin (impaired CMI), multiple asymmetric lesions, and nerve involvement. LL has negative lepromin but tends to have symmetric lesions and the highest BI.

questions.q: A 25-year-old sexually active man presents with a painless, indurated, single ulcer on the coronal sulcus. The ulcer has a clean base and rolled edges. Darkfield microscopy shows motile corkscrew organisms. What is the recommended first-line treatment?
opts: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM single dose
questions.exp: The clinical picture is primary syphilis (painless indurated chancre, positive darkfield for Treponema pallidum). First-line treatment is benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM as a single dose. Doxycycline is an alternative for penicillin-allergic patients.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman with butterfly-shaped erythema on the face, photosensitivity, and arthralgia has a positive ANA (1:640, speckled pattern). Her anti-dsDNA is positive and complement levels are low. The histopathological finding in the involved skin that is MOST specific for this diagnosis is:
opts: Vacuolar degeneration of basal layer with thickened basement membrane
questions.exp: In SLE (and lupus erythematosus in general), the most specific histopathological finding is vacuolar/hydropic degeneration of the basal cell layer combined with thickening of the epidermal basement membrane (PAS-positive). The lupus band (immunoglobulin/complement deposits at the DEJ on DIF) is also specific but is an immunofluorescence finding.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man presents with tense bullae on normal and erythematous skin, predominantly on the lower abdomen and thighs. Nikolsky sign is negative. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 deposits at the dermoepidermal junction. The target antigen is:
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid (BP) is characterized by tense bullae, negative Nikolsky sign, and linear IgG/C3 at the BMZ on DIF. The primary autoantigen is BP180 (BPAG2/type XVII collagen), specifically the NC16A domain. BP230 (BPAG1) is also targeted but less important. BP180 is the main target.

questions.q: A 60-year-old presents with an 8 mm pearly translucent nodule with telangiectasias on the nose, slowly growing over 2 years. Histopathology shows nests of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading and retraction artifact. What is the risk of metastasis from this tumour?
questions.exp: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most common skin malignancy and has an extremely low metastatic potential of <0.1% (often cited as 0.0028-0.55%). It is locally destructive (rodent ulcer) but rarely spreads to lymph nodes or distant sites.

questions.q: A dermatologist performs a punch biopsy. The punch is inserted with rotating motion to what depth before withdrawing to ensure adequate subcutaneous fat for diagnosis of panniculitis?
questions.exp: For panniculitis evaluation, the punch biopsy must extend into the subcutaneous fat. The punch (typically 4-6 mm) is rotated with downward pressure until the hub is nearly at skin level to reach fat. Going only to dermis is adequate for inflammatory dermatoses but insufficient for panniculitis diagnosis.

questions.q: A patient on long-term dapsone therapy for dermatitis herpetiformis develops haemolytic anaemia and methaemoglobinaemia. Which co-administered drug reduces these side effects?
questions.exp: Cimetidine (a CYP2C8/CYP3A4 inhibitor) reduces the N-hydroxylation of dapsone by hepatic cytochrome P450, thereby decreasing the formation of hydroxylamine metabolites responsible for methaemoglobinaemia and haemolysis. It is the recommended drug to reduce these adverse effects.

questions.q: A 19-year-old man has multiple comedones, papules, and nodules on the face and trunk. He is started on isotretinoin. Which of the following is a mandatory monitoring parameter during therapy?
questions.exp: Isotretinoin commonly causes hypertriglyceridaemia (and less commonly hypercholesterolaemia). Fasting lipid profile should be obtained at baseline and monitored (typically at 4-8 weeks) during therapy. Liver function tests are also monitored. LFTs and lipids are the key mandatory parameters.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with thickened, fissured, darkened skin in the axillae and neck with a velvety texture. She is obese with a BMI of 38. The most important investigation to request next is:
opts: Fasting plasma glucose and insulin levels
questions.exp: Acanthosis nigricans in an obese patient is most commonly associated with insulin resistance. The priority investigation is fasting plasma glucose and fasting insulin to assess for insulin resistance/type 2 diabetes. Biopsy is rarely needed; typical histology shows papillomatosis and hyperkeratosis.

questions.q: A newborn presents with widespread blistering from birth with minimal trauma. Electron microscopy shows cleavage at the level of the lamina lucida. The gene most likely mutated is:
questions.exp: Cleavage in the lamina lucida (between the hemidesmosome lower plate and the lamina densa) is characteristic of junctional EB (JEB). LAMB3 (encoding laminin beta-3/laminin 332) is the most commonly mutated gene in JEB. COL7A1 mutations cause dystrophic EB (sublamina densa cleavage); KRT5/14 cause simplex EB (intraepidermal); COL17A1 also causes JEB but less commonly.

questions.q: A 30-year-old presents with multiple café-au-lait macules (>6, each >15 mm), axillary freckling, and a palpable subcutaneous nodule on the forearm. Which of the following cutaneous features is considered pathognomonic for this condition?
questions.exp: Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas seen on slit-lamp examination) are pathognomonic for Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1). While café-au-lait macules, axillary freckling, and neurofibromas are diagnostic criteria, they are not individually pathognomonic. Lisch nodules are not seen in any other condition.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman with no prior history presents with sudden onset of patchy hair loss forming a well-defined oval patch on the scalp. There is no scaling. Hair pull test shows exclamation mark hairs at the periphery. The immunopathogenesis involves:
opts: Type II hypersensitivity with anti-hair follicle IgG
CD8+ T cell-mediated collapse of immune privilege of hair follicle
Neutrophilic destruction of hair follicle stem cells
questions.exp: Alopecia areata results from collapse of the immune privilege of the hair follicle. Autoreactive CD8+ NKG2D+ T cells target melanocyte-associated autoantigens (e.g., melanin, tyrosinase) in the follicular bulb. The hair follicle normally evades immune attack due to low MHC-I expression and local immunosuppressive factors. JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib) that block this pathway are now approved.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man presents with a 3-year history of salmon-pink scaly plaques on the scalp and extensor surfaces with nail pitting and oncholysis. He now develops bilateral knee swelling with morning stiffness. Which HLA type is most strongly associated with psoriatic arthritis?
questions.exp: HLA-B27 is most strongly associated with psoriatic arthritis (particularly the axial/spondyloarthropathy pattern). HLA-Cw6 is most strongly associated with plaque psoriasis itself (especially early-onset, guttate type). HLA-B27 association with PsA is comparable to its role in ankylosing spondylitis.

questions.q: A 5-year-old child develops a painful, rapidly enlarging boggy swelling on the scalp with overlying alopecia, pustules, and cervical lymphadenopathy after playing with a puppy. The most appropriate treatment is:
opts: Oral griseofulvin for 6-8 weeks with topical antifungal shampoo
questions.exp: The presentation is kerion (inflammatory tinea capitis), most commonly caused by Microsporum canis or Trichophyton mentagrophytes (zoophilic). Treatment requires systemic antifungal because topicals do not penetrate the hair shaft. Griseofulvin remains the first-line for tinea capitis in children (6-8 weeks). Adjunct antifungal shampoo reduces shedding/transmission.

questions.q: A 35-year-old HIV-positive patient (CD4 count 50 cells/μL) presents with deeply pigmented, indurated papules and nodules distributed on the lower extremities, face, and oral mucosa. Histopathology shows a poorly differentiated spindle cell proliferation with slit-like vascular spaces and extravasated red cells. The causative virus is:
questions.exp: Kaposi sarcoma in AIDS patients (epidemic/AIDS-associated KS) is caused by HHV-8 (Human Herpesvirus 8, Kaposi Sarcoma Herpesvirus). It presents with violaceous/pigmented lesions and spindle cell vascular proliferation on histology. HHV-8 is latently present in all forms of KS and is necessary (though not sufficient) for its development.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with target lesions on the palms and feet, erosions of the buccal mucosa, and conjunctival injection. She took a sulfonamide antibiotic 10 days ago for a urinary infection. What is the drug of choice for immunosuppressive management in the acute phase?
opts: Supportive care only; corticosteroids are contraindicated
questions.exp: Cyclosporine is the preferred immunosuppressive agent in Stevens-Johnson syndrome/Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis. It acts by blocking T-cell mediated keratinocyte apoptosis (via calcineurin inhibition). Corticosteroids are controversial and potentially harmful. IVIG showed benefit in early studies but meta-analyses show variable results. Cyclosporine has the best evidence in recent studies.

questions.q: A 40-year-old presents with multiple skin-coloured papules in the malar and nasolabial fold areas, periungual fibromas, and ash-leaf macules. MRI brain shows cortical tubers. Mutation in which gene leads to the most severe renal manifestations in this condition?
questions.exp: Tuberous sclerosis complex is caused by mutations in TSC1 (hamartin, chromosome 9) or TSC2 (tuberin, chromosome 16). TSC2 mutations are generally associated with more severe disease, including more frequent and severe renal angiomyolipomas, renal cysts, and renal cell carcinoma. TSC2 also shows more severe neurological involvement.

questions.q: A 50-year-old male presents with discrete hypopigmented macules on the trunk, scattered symmetrically. Wood's lamp examination shows ivory-white fluorescence. Scraping shows fine adherent scales. KOH prep shows 'spaghetti and meatballs' appearance. The causative organism requires which nutritional supplement to grow in culture?
questions.exp: The description is pityriasis versicolor caused by Malassezia furfur (and other Malassezia spp.). Malassezia are lipophilic yeasts that are part of normal skin flora and require exogenous lipids (long-chain fatty acids, typically olive oil) for in vitro culture on Sabouraud's medium. This is because they lack the ability to synthesize C12-C14 fatty acids.

questions.q: A 32-year-old presents with grouped vesicles and crusts on the extensor aspects of elbows and knees, with intense pruritus. Direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin shows granular IgA deposits at the dermoepidermal junction. This patient should be screened for:
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) with granular IgA deposits at the BMZ is strongly associated with gluten-sensitive enteropathy (coeliac disease) in nearly 100% of patients, though the bowel disease may be clinically silent. Strict gluten-free diet improves both skin and gut disease. Anti-tissue transglutaminase and anti-endomysial antibodies are positive.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with hardening of skin of the hands and face, Raynaud phenomenon, dysphagia, and telangiectasias. ANA shows nucleolar pattern. Her anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) is strongly positive. What is the most feared complication in anti-Scl-70 positive patients?
questions.exp: Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) antibodies are associated with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis and carry a high risk of interstitial lung disease (ILD), which is the leading cause of morbidity/mortality in anti-Scl-70 positive patients. In contrast, anti-centromere antibodies are associated with limited SSc and PAH.

questions.q: A mother brings her 8-year-old boy who has had recurrent skin and lymph node abscesses caused by Staphylococcus aureus and Aspergillus. NBT (nitroblue tetrazolium) test is abnormal. Flow cytometry shows markedly reduced DHR (dihydrorhodamine) oxidation. Which pathway is defective?
questions.exp: The clinical picture of recurrent catalase-positive organism infections (S. aureus, Aspergillus) with abnormal NBT/DHR test is classic for Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD). The defect is in the NADPH oxidase complex (typically gp91phox encoded by CYBB on X-chromosome), which is responsible for the respiratory burst in neutrophils/macrophages.

questions.q: During MOHS micrographic surgery, the surgeon maps and colour-codes each tissue section. What is the key advantage of MOHS over standard excision for basal cell carcinoma?
opts: Lower recurrence rate due to intraoperative 100% margin examination
Applicable to all body sites without modification
questions.exp: MOHS micrographic surgery achieves 5-year cure rates of >99% for primary BCC because it allows complete (100%) examination of surgical margins intraoperatively (horizontal frozen sections). Standard excision examines only 1-5% of margins (bread-loaf sections). This allows tissue sparing while ensuring complete tumour removal, making it ideal for high-risk/recurrent BCC.

questions.q: A 22-year-old presents with tender, erythematous nodules over the anterior shins bilaterally. She had a sore throat 2 weeks ago. CXR shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Skin biopsy shows septal panniculitis without vasculitis. This combination of findings in a young woman most likely represents:
questions.exp: Lofgren's syndrome is an acute presentation of sarcoidosis characterized by the triad of: bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, erythema nodosum (septal panniculitis on histology), and periarticular inflammation (fever, arthralgia). It predominantly affects young women and has a good prognosis with spontaneous resolution. The preceding sore throat can be a trigger.

questions.q: A 38-year-old man presents with a non-healing ulcer on the dorsal foot that has been present for 6 weeks, with raised indurated edges and a granulomatous base. He recently returned from a trip to the Amazon rainforest. PCR confirms Leishmania braziliensis. The major concern with this species compared to L. donovani is:
questions.exp: Leishmania braziliensis causes New World cutaneous leishmaniasis and has a significant risk (up to 5%) of mucocutaneous extension (espundia) — spread to nasal and oral mucosa causing severe destructive lesions. L. donovani causes visceral leishmaniasis and PKDL. Treatment of L. braziliensis is with systemic antimonials or amphotericin B due to this risk.

questions.q: A 25-year-old presents with a single painless ulcer on the genitalia. VDRL is non-reactive but FTA-ABS is reactive. Darkfield microscopy is negative. The most appropriate next step is:
opts: Treat as primary syphilis and repeat VDRL in 4 weeks
Diagnose as false-positive FTA-ABS and discharge
Perform T. pallidum IgM ELISA and repeat serologies in 2 weeks
questions.exp: In early primary syphilis, non-treponemal tests (VDRL, RPR) may be non-reactive (seroconversion takes 1-3 weeks post-ulcer), but treponemal tests (FTA-ABS) become positive first. A reactive FTA-ABS with a genital ulcer is sufficient to diagnose primary syphilis and initiate treatment. Repeating VDRL in 4 weeks will confirm seroconversion. Treatment is not withheld.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman presents with generalized pruritus and violaceous flat-topped polygonal papules on the wrists and ankles with fine white lines on the surface. Biopsy shows a saw-tooth pattern of rete ridges with a band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at the DEJ and civatte bodies. First-line treatment for symptomatic disease is:
questions.exp: Lichen planus is characterized by Wickham's striae (fine white lines due to focal hypergranulosis), saw-tooth acanthosis, band-like lymphocytic infiltrate, and civatte bodies (colloid/hyaline bodies from apoptotic keratinocytes). First-line treatment for localized cutaneous LP is potent or superpotent topical corticosteroids. Systemic steroids are used for severe/extensive disease.

questions.q: A patient with type I neurofibromatosis develops a rapidly growing plexiform neurofibroma with pain. MRI shows a heterogeneous lesion with displacement of surrounding structures. The FDA-approved drug targeting the MEK pathway for this indication is:
questions.exp: Selumetinib (a MEK1/2 inhibitor) is FDA-approved for children with NF1 and symptomatic inoperable plexiform neurofibromas. NF1 encodes neurofibromin (a RAS-GAP), and its loss leads to hyperactivation of the RAS/MAPK pathway. MEK is downstream of RAS, making MEK inhibition an effective strategy. Everolimus targets mTOR and is used for TSC.

questions.q: A 40-year-old presents with yellow discolouration of all fingernails, transverse ridging, and absence of lunula. He has a chronic cough with productive sputum. Which underlying condition is most commonly associated with this nail disorder?
questions.exp: Yellow nail syndrome is characterized by the triad of yellow/thickened slow-growing nails (with absent lunula and loss of cuticle), lymphoedema, and respiratory manifestations (pleural effusion, bronchiectasis, sinusitis). It is thought to result from impaired lymphatic drainage. All three features are present in only ~30% of cases; the combination of yellow nails + respiratory disease is most common.
